newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-Political deaths rise in S.Africa's Zulu province.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Political deaths rise in S.Africa's Zulu province.

text.p: "Oh Mandela, you are bringing us peace," sang thousands of African National Congress supporters in South Africa's troubled KwaZulu-Natal province.
But the rising number of political deaths tells another story.
Political violence in KwaZulu-Natal, home to nine million Zulus, is flaring up again after months of relative peace, monitors said.

At least 98 people have been killed since the beginning of the year, with 20 people murdered in the first three weeks of May and 34 deaths in April, in the region where ANC supporters have battled with rivals from the Inkatha Freedom Party.

Although the death toll was nowhere near its peak of 338 in April 1994, when South Africans of all races cast their vote, it is climbing steadily again, according to researchers at the independent Human Rights Committee.
"There has been a resurgence of political killings and violence over the past two months. We are not exactly sure why," researcher Jessica McKay told Reuters.
She said most of the violence was, as before, between President Nelson Mandela's ANC and Inkatha, but there were also fierce intra-party struggles for power in some areas.
MANDELA'S VISIT TO BOOST ANC IN RURAL AREAS
Mandela visited the hilly Midlands area in May to bolster the ANC's standing in rural areas where the Zulu-traditionalist Inkatha, led by Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi, holds sway.
The ANC won KwaZulu's major cities and towns in local elections in June last year, but Inkatha won the overall provincial vote on its rural base.
A year-old peace treaty signed days ahead of the local government elections seems to be faltering.
Bitter turf wars over the past decade between the ANC and Inkatha have killed more than 14,000 people and left up to half a million homeless.

The provincial ANC, with Mandela's suppport, has drawn up a secret peace package, which includes a proposal for special amnesty for perpetrators of violence in KwaZulu-Natal, and has recently presented it to Inkatha, party sources said.
Inkatha said it had not received anything in writing but talks would continue with the ANC to "detail the nature of the proposals and the parameters of the negotiation process".
Mandela told a rally of 4,000 party faithful at the end of May that he supported the peace initiative.
"I sincerely support the sentiments behind this initiative, and I salute the provincial leader of both parties for these efforts," he said.
With relative peace in the province, Mandela's government has been concentrating instead on tackling violent crime that is plaguing South Africa and deterring investors.
RENEGADE STEALS ANC SUPPORTERS

A political analyst said another reason for Mandela's visit to the Midlands was to curtail support for former ANC leader Sifiso Nkabinde, who was recently thrown out of the party for allegedly spying on the organisation for apartheid-era police.
Nkabinde has sided with another ANC outcast, Bantu Holomisa, who hopes to form a new party. Nkabinde took with him thousands of supporters in his Richmond stronghold.
Mandela was jeered and booed by hundreds of Nkabinde fans on a visit to Richmond for the funeral of an ANC councillor.

"It is nothing new for Mandela to be booed and for crowds to react negatively to him. It would be true to say that his sureness of touch does not always extend to KwaZulu-Natal," said Alexander Johnston, politics professor at the University of Natal.
He said it would take more than visits aimed at improving the ANC's standing in rural areas ahead of the 1999 national elections to bring peace to KwaZulu-Natal.

"Both Inkatha and the ANC will have to bring the loose cannons in their organisations under control. It will be very difficult to forge a lasting peace if there are elements who are dubious in their allegiance to their parties," Johnston said.
